## Abstract

Historical evidence shows that environmental issues have been secondary to United States’ agricultural policy since the first farm bill in 1933. The farm sector has undergone massive changes in technology and farming practices, but the environmental problems it causes have remained ancillary to productivist goals. Agri-environmental policy has continued to rely on subsidies and voluntary farmer participation, while combining environmental objectives with price and income support aims. The faith of agri-environmental programs is largely determined by what is desirable for safety net purposes, and in times of high crop and livestock prices and increased environmental pressures conservation is particularly underfunded. Additionally, monitoring and program assessment are poorly structured. This is particularly concerning today given the threats of climate change and agriculture’s contribution to it. A major rethinking of these taxpayer-funded programs is necessary to improve their effectiveness. Programs should focus on environmental outcomes and monitoring and assessment should be strengthened.

Keywords: Agri-environmental policies, Climate change mitigation, Environmental governance, Policy assessment

## Introduction

There have been enormous changes to the US agricultural sector since the establishment of the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) in 1862: the country has gone from being an agriculture-based economy to one in which agriculture contributes less than 1% of the Gross Domestic Product and employs about 1% of the labor force (Gierlinger and Krausmann 2012; Kassel and Morrison 2020). Agricultural policies in general have changed in response to market conditions, and also driven many of farming’s structural shifts (Fig. 1 and Table 1).

Even though the tools being used in agricultural policy in the US have changed, the focus has remained on supporting farmers’ income via subsidizing prices and revenues. The first phase started in 1933 with the first farm bill, in response to the Great Depression and the Dust Bowl, and relied on supply management. If prices went below a certain level, farmers received subsidies, but they had to agree to limit planted acreage for specific crops. The subsidies were determined using the parity concept, based on the equality of exchange between agriculture and other economic sectors in a “normal period”. The government acted as a buyer of last resort for excess stocks. This approach, coupled with increases in productivity due to enormous technological changes, caused massive food surpluses which depressed prices, but was viable in the high export periods of War World II and the Korean War. However, it became untenable in the 1960s, and levels of support were reduced to address overproduction and budget outlays. In 1973, with high prices and record exports, target prices linked to world prices started to be used to determine subsidy levels, while set asides and reserves continued. Policy changed further in the 1980s, as support levels were reduced, and the government shifted away from being the buyer of last resort and increased planting flexibility. This movement towards flexibility reached its peak in the 1996 farm bill, which corresponded to another high crop prices period. Subsidies were de-linked from prices into fixed payments. However, when prices fell soon after, ad hoc payments were instituted and then became permanent as countercyclical payments. Direct payments continued as well until 2014, when crop insurance became the primary commodity subsidy tool (Bowers et al. 1984; Gardner 1992; Glauber and Effland 2016; Coppess 2018). Throughout this period and till today, agri-environmental policies1 have remained ancillary to the productivist philosophy that has driven the commodity subsidies, using ineffective mechanisms that have only marginally adapted to massive changes in technology and farming practices, as the timeline in Table 1 illustrates. In fact, the two tenets of US agricultural conservation have remained the same since before the first farm bill.

First, the policies rely on a voluntary approach to participation and subsidies. This makes it impossible to target specific landscape problems. Most policies are field-based, so conservation in one field can be offset by production-enhancing activities elsewhere on the farm. The combination of field-based conservation and commodity subsidies is the reason why land set aside programs, instituted in the 1930s and 1950s to prop up falling prices, failed: farmers substituted capital (often the very capital provided by the conservation subsidies) for land, therefore at the farm level production increased and so did negative environmental outcomes. This leakage or spillage, in which the direct effects of a program are offset by indirect ones that the program set in motion (Engel et al. 2008), has beset US conservation since the start.

In a productivist setting like the US, these policies also trigger a technological treadmill: farmers improve their incomes by adopting new technologies, temporarily increasing their profits and squeezing out smaller “laggard” farmers (Cochrane 1979, Levins and Cochrane 1996). This brings us to the second tenet: most US agricultural conservation policies are dual-goal. That is, they combine environmental objectives with price or income support ones (Batie 1985; Secchi et al. 2008). Therefore, their faith is largely determined by what is desirable for safety net purposes. If prices are low, conservation activities get more funding to support farm incomes. Conversely, when prices are high, there is no need to support incomes and conservation activities are reduced, as also become more expensive since, to the extent they reduce yields, their opportunity cost is higher. Because the activities are dual-goal, often conservation programs fund ineffective practices, and larger farms receive more support (Mishra and Khanal 2013).

The existing literature has generally focused on shorter periods of time and not looked at the whole historical trajectory of US agri-environmental policy and its linkages with the farm economy. The 1930s, the 1950–1960s and the 1980s saw both dramatic challenges for the farm sector and declining prices, and corresponded to large increases in agri-environmental spending (Fig. 2). Conversely, in time of high prices, conservation spending declined or was shifted to activities that still allowed high production levels and were not very effective. For example, the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) is a land retirement policy that was instituted in 1985 during the farm crisis. The program pays farmers to take cropland out of production for 10 to 15 years to go in perennial vegetation (grassland or forest). Before the ethanol boom, academics were positing that the benefits of the program would last beyond the end of the contracts and farmers would keep CRP land out of production (Roberts and Lubowski 2007). However, as crop prices rose after 2007, the acreage cap on the land that could be enrolled in the program was severely restricted and much of the land was plowed at the end of the contract period (Bigelow et al. 2020). Historically grounded assessments of the CRP would have been more helpful in planning for a policy response in the event of high prices. Instead, in the boom period, conservation funding shifted to existing working land programs, while monitoring to ensure farmers were following appropriate conservation practices remained a problem (Stubbs 2010; Holland et al. 2020). The reallocation to working land conservation was hailed as an example of “ecological modernization” (Reimer 2015). However, a recent assessment found that the largest working land program mostly funds low-potential practices (Basche et al. 2020). US working land conservation programs have been plagued by ineffectiveness issues because of program design features that still persist. Bearing in mind the historical context could improve program effectiveness.

Here, I consider US conservation programs from their inception to show that there has never been a fundamental realignment in priorities to effectively address the environmental impacts of productivist agriculture, and that in fact agri-environmental policies largely respond to productivist concerns. This continuity in policy approach is due to “technological optimism”, which results in new technologies being seen as the solutions to environmental problems (Gaskell et al. 2001). The US approach is to devote considerable financial resources to “patch up” immediate, smaller scale issues without addressing systemic sustainability challenges (Buttel 2006).2 Characteristics of the US political economy also contribute to the persistence of the approach. Political scientists have found that corporate interests play a big role in farm bill negotiations via campaign contributions, and they prefer high-input, industrialized systems (Sheingate et al. 2017). In this respect, ideas such as post productivism and multifunctionality (Wilson 2001; Ilbery and Bowler 2014) being considered in the European Union (EU) and other countries in the global North are still quite marginal in the United States.

The continued ineffectiveness of conservation policies is particularly concerning since agriculture is a disproportionate contributor to climate change. In the US, it generates over 10% of Green House Gas (GHG) emissions (USEPA 2022). The increased dependence of industrial agriculture on fossil fuels has also meant that the GHG emissions attributable to US agriculture have increased, even though emissions from land use change have decreased after the beginning of the twentieth century (Höhne et al. 2011). A critical reassessment of these policies and the system they help perpetuate is a necessary first step to move towards a more sustainable agricultural sector (Weis 2010), and to address the dominant narrative of industrial agriculture as a production system of “stewards of the land” (Ruhl 2002). A pressing issue is that conservation subsidies and dual-goal policies are now starting to be used in agricultural climate mitigation policy. The ineffectiveness of agri-environmental policies must be addressed if agriculture is to become part of the solution to climate change.
